title: Before You Trust an AI Agent With Your Accounts
summary: AI agents can now manage your email, calendar, and finances. But the same features that make them useful also make them risky. Here is what to check before granting access.
before: Could only read and respond. The worst outcome was a bad answer or embarrassing output.
after: Can read, write, and act across connected accounts. A mistake or attack can move money, delete data, or send messages.
body:
AI agents are no longer just answering questions. They are booking flights, managing calendars, sending emails, and in some cases handling financial transactions on your behalf. That capability is genuinely useful. It is also genuinely risky. Before you connect an agent to your accounts, you should understand what can go wrong and how to protect yourself.

If you want the technical background on how agents work, see our explainer on agentic-ai-explained. This article focuses on the practical safety questions you should ask before granting access.

## The Difference Between Read Access and Act Access

When an agent asks for permission to connect to your email, calendar, or bank account, pay attention to what kind of access it is requesting. There is a meaningful difference between an agent that can read your data and one that can act on it.

Read access lets an agent see information: your inbox, your calendar events, your transaction history. That is useful for answering questions and generating summaries. But the risk is limited. If something goes wrong, the agent might leak information it should not have seen, but it cannot change anything.

Write access (sometimes called "act access") is different. An agent with write permissions can send emails, schedule meetings, move money, or delete files. The blast radius of a mistake or attack is much larger. As one security guide puts it, "read access and write access are different risks and should be granted independently."

The practical advice: start with read-only permissions whenever possible. Only grant write access when you genuinely need the agent to take actions, and even then, prefer narrow permissions over broad ones.

## How Prompt Injection Becomes Your Problem

Prompt injection is the core vulnerability that makes agent safety hard. We cover the mechanics in detail elsewhere, but the short version is this: LLMs cannot reliably tell the difference between your instructions and malicious instructions hidden in content they process.

This matters because agents read things. They read your emails, web pages, documents, and API responses. If an attacker embeds hidden instructions in any of that content, the agent might follow those instructions instead of yours.

This is not theoretical. Security researchers have documented malicious prompts hidden in website meta tags, code repository comments, and even email bodies. In one case, attackers embedded hidden instructions designed to redirect financial actions toward attacker-controlled endpoints. In another, hidden CSS commands in web content tricked AI coding assistants into exfiltrating developer API keys.

The risk scales with what the agent can do. An agent with read-only access that gets tricked might leak some information. An agent with payment capabilities that gets tricked could send money to the wrong place.

## Permission Prompts Are Not Security Theater (If You Read Them)

Most well-designed agent platforms now show you permission prompts before connecting to your accounts. These screens tell you exactly what the agent will be able to access and what actions it can take.

Treat these prompts seriously. Look for:

- **Scope of access**: Is the agent requesting access to one inbox or all your Google accounts? One spreadsheet or your entire Drive?
- **Read vs. write**: Can it only view your calendar, or can it also create, modify, and delete events?
- **Duration**: Is this a one-time access or permanent until you revoke it?
- **Sensitive actions**: Does it mention sending emails, making purchases, or accessing financial data?

If the permissions seem broader than what you need the agent to do, that is a red flag. A scheduling agent does not need access to your bank account. A research assistant does not need permission to send emails on your behalf.

## Why "Human in the Loop" Matters

The safest agent configurations require your approval before taking high-stakes actions. This is sometimes called "human in the loop" or step-up authentication.

Look for agents that ask for confirmation before:

- Sending messages to other people
- Making purchases or financial transactions
- Deleting or permanently modifying data
- Sharing information externally

This adds friction, which is the point. The friction gives you a chance to catch mistakes or manipulation before they cause real damage. An agent that deletes a production database without asking is not more convenient. It is more dangerous.

## What Good Platforms Do Differently

Not all agent platforms take safety equally seriously. When evaluating a new tool, look for:

- **Granular permission controls**: Can you grant access to specific folders, accounts, or actions rather than everything?
- **Short-lived credentials**: Does the platform use temporary access tokens that expire, or permanent keys that live forever?
- **Audit logs**: Can you see what the agent actually did with your accounts?
- **Easy revocation**: Can you cut off access immediately if something goes wrong?

These features do not eliminate risk, but they limit the damage when something inevitably goes sideways.

## The Bottom Line

AI agents are powerful precisely because they can do things on your behalf. That same power is what makes them risky. Before you connect an agent to your accounts, ask yourself: if this agent made a mistake or got tricked, what is the worst thing it could do with these permissions?

If the answer makes you uncomfortable, narrow the permissions. Start with read-only access. Require confirmation for sensitive actions. And pay attention to those permission prompts. They are the last line of defense between a helpful assistant and an expensive mistake.
